prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and contract setting, and policy rules and microfounded welfare analysis that underpin the modern framework for monetary policy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement B014 prize to Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. After round 1 I tested it against the chair's question of whether I can defend the trio on stated criteria rather than on support counts. I think I can. Each name corresponds to a separable, datable building block: the time-dependent pricing device (Calvo), staggered contracts and an interest-rate rule (Taylor), and the microfounded, welfare-based policy framework (Woodford). Each has an identifiable originating body of work, and each has had 25 to 40 years of use, extension and criticism, so maturity is not in question. The framework is now the common language of monetary policy analysis, so breadth of consequence is very large. I would accept a citation confined to nominal-rigidity theory, policy rules and the welfare-based policy framework. That is the wording I now propose. It deliberately avoids any claim about forecasting performance or about a particular Phillips-curve specification, which answers the post-2008 and post-2021 concerns on the citation side. One thing did move: I now treat B032 as my first fallback rather than B042. Round 1 sharpened the maturity and credit-line case for Autor, Dorn and Hanson on the trade-shock evidence. It also sharpened the empirical-anchor and 2022-overlap reservations about B042, which I share.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is still the main weakness, and round 1 did not remove it. Eight names are credited, so a three-person cap leaves out Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose Phillips-curve, policy-analysis and estimated medium-scale model work made the framework quantitatively usable. Whether the Committee wants to honour the theoretical originators or the estimation strand is a judgement, not a fact, and no argument I have read settles it. The framework's empirical performance after 2008 and in 2021 to 2023 is also contested, and a prize could be misread as endorsing the baseline model. Finally, I am a macroeconomist and my field is close to this candidate, so I may be a poor judge of how crowded the area looks from outside.

responses.point: Andersson moved from B007 to B014 in round 1 and proposes the same trio. He would give Galí more weight than his own proposal does, and he words the citation around nominal rigidities and the policy-analysis framework, with no claim about forecasting performance. He concedes that omitting Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost of the three-person cut.
responses.response: We agree on the citation, and I adopt his restraint. The text should rest on rigidities, rules and the welfare-based policy framework, and say nothing about the Phillips-curve slope or forecasting. On Galí, I would weigh him heavily if the Committee decided to honour the estimation and synthesis strand. But Galí's contribution builds on Calvo pricing and overlaps with Woodford's synthesis in what it demonstrates, so under a three-person cap I would not drop an originator for him. I also think we should be honest that this is a decision about which layer to credit. It is not a discovery about who mattered more. If the Committee settles on the estimation strand, I would not call the Galí, Gertler and Woodford cut indefensible. I would still prefer to credit the building blocks first.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B014 sixth and proposes Woodford, Galí and Gertler as the most synthetic contributors. He stresses the credit-allocation problem across eight names, mixed evidence on the Phillips curve, and the risk that earlier macro prizes already cover nearby ground. He prefers B010 for its cleaner two-person attribution.
responses.response: His diagnosis of the attribution problem is right, and I do not treat B014's difficulty as small. Our difference is in the remedy. A Woodford, Galí and Gertler trio rewards the synthesis and application layer but omits the originators of the two ingredients that define the framework, staggered pricing and the policy rule with staggered contracts. Mixed Phillips-curve evidence argues for a citation built on rigidities and rules, not for crediting the later empirical strand. I also accept that B010 has the tidier credit line, and I would not oppose it on merit. I rank B014 above it because of breadth of consequence. The mechanism is used across policy institutions, whereas the size of the selection-based welfare gains in B010 depends on functional-form choices that he and Krusell both flag. I regard this as a weighting judgement between attribution cleanliness and reach, and I do not claim it is decisive.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B032 first with Autor, Hanson and Dorn, moved from Katz to Dorn on attribution grounds. She frames the citation around technology and trade shocks with the China-shock evidence as the identified core. She accepts that the task framework also depends on people outside the list and that magnitude and persistence of the trade-shock effects remain debated.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case, which is why B032 is now my first alternative. Her narrowing of the citation to the identified local labour-market evidence addresses most of my round-1 worry about splitting credit between the task theory and the trade-shock work. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are a coherent attribution unit. The chair's question was what would move me. If the Committee agrees the citation covers the trade-shock evidence only, and the B014 cut proves unresolvable on the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford versus Galí-Gertler question, I would support B032 over a contested B014. My remaining hesitation is that I cannot independently judge the latest re-examinations of shift-share inference and persistence. Dreber Almenberg and Teorell say the same about their own knowledge. I would want the Committee to rely on the qualitative local-adjustment findings and not on aggregate magnitudes. I do not think the Katz exclusion is trivial, but it follows from the same strand-separation logic I apply to B014.

responses.point: Teorell moved from B042 to B032 and keeps B042 as his first alternative. He leaves B014 out of his alternatives because, with eight credited names, he cannot defend a particular trio. He also weights the reservation that direct identification of the collateral channel is mixed and that the 2022 overlap cuts against B042.
responses.response: I accept that B014 asks the Committee to defend a trio among eight names, and that this is a harder task than for Kiyotaki and Moore. I would still say that difficulty is not equivalent to indefensibility. The trio rests on three stated criteria: the originator of a distinct building block, separability from the neighbouring strands, and durability over decades. Those can be applied transparently to any substitution, including Galí or Gertler. On B042, his shift toward weighting the empirical-anchor point matches my own. I regard the collateral mechanism as foundational theory, but its direct identification is weaker than the policy footprint of the nominal-rigidity framework. I read the 2022 prize as covering banking and financial-crisis theory and evidence, not collateral-constraint amplification, though this is my recollection and I cannot verify it here. B042 therefore remains a fallback, not something I would elevate.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants to honour the theoretical originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or the estimation and synthesis strand (Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets). I cannot resolve this from the exchange, and it is the main reason my preferred part could fail.
How much the post-2008 and 2021 to 2023 inflation experience should weigh against the framework, as opposed to shaping the citation wording.

Whether the evidence behind B032, in particular the persistence of China-shock effects and shift-share inference, is as mature as its supporters say. I rely on their accounts and my own limited knowledge.
Whether the 2022 prize overlap with B042 is complementary or redundant, based on members' stated recollections that I have not verified.

Whether support is spread across B014, B032, B010 and B016 so evenly that none can reach six votes. I treat that as a procedural fact, not as evidence about merit, and I do not change my configuration to manufacture consensus.
statement.conflict_note: I am a frequent co-author with Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author with John Hassler (chair), and I am an IIES colleague of both. Krusell and I prefer B014, and Hassler lists it as an alternative. I am also one of the three explicit B014 supporters in the chair's summary. None of Calvo, Taylor or Woodford, nor Kiyotaki and Moore, nor Autor, Dorn and Hanson, is a documented co-author of mine. I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (B030, which is not in my configuration) and with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li, none of whom is credited on my configuration or alternatives. My research field, macroeconomics and growth, is close to B014 and B042, which may bias my sense of how crowded the area is. I apply common criteria and disclose this without adjudicating it. Prior-prize facts mentioned here are members' stated recollections and have not been verified.
